newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Unionist Trimble castigates rivals.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Unionist Trimble castigates rivals.

text.p: Chief pro-British politician David Trimble accused rival Protestant leaders on Saturday of damaging Northern Ireland's union with Britain.

Firing a broadside to win Protestant moderate votes in the May 1 election, Trimble castigated firebrand Protestant Ian Paisley and another Unionist, Robert McCartney, for hardline attitudes which he said had backfired on "Unionism".
"The reasonable case we present is being obscured by aggressive, loudmouth unionists," he told his Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) annual conference in a keynote speech.
"This is not in the interests of the Union. It is not what the Unionist people want."
Trimble's UUP, which currently holds nine of the province's 17 seats in the British parliament, is backed by most of the Protestant majority population.
The campaign is being fought amid tension because Irish Republican Army guerrillas refuse to call off a war against rule from London and a Protestant guerrilla truce is unstable.

The UUP is locked in a bitter struggle for votes with Paisley's Democratic Unionist Party which traditionally takes a diehard approach to maintaining Union with Britain and scorns links with neighbouring Catholic Ireland.
A fundamentalist Protestant preacher as well as politician, Paisley is one of the DUP's three members of parliament.
Robert McCartney, a parliamentarian who leads the tiny United Kingdom Unionist Party, is a stern opponent of the UUP.
Trimble derided Paisley for indulging in exaggerated "slogans and pantomimes" that have won him a reputation as Northern Ireland's most uncompromising advocate of British rule.

"I disagree with the McCartneys and Paisleys. Their actions and attitudes have been counter-productive. They have let nationalists off the hook. They have driven London into the arms of Dublin," Trimble said.
"Unfortunately the methods of those who denigrate us continue to do damage to the Union at home, in the rest of the United Kingdom (Britain) and elsewhere."
Trimble urged Catholics and Protestants to leave the past behind and agree new institutions.
He proposed a new Northern Ireland Assembly, under Britain, in which Protestant and Catholic representatives would have influential roles based on the votes won by their parties.
